title: Fusulina whorls increase in ratio 1:1.5, a spiral of constant angle about 86°

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Fusulina whorls increase in ratio 1:1.5, a spiral of constant angle about 86°

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In Fusulina the breadths of successive whorls stand in the nearly constant ratio 1 : 1.5, which corresponds to a logarithmic spiral with a constant angle of about 86°, like that of ammonites.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: And this ratio of 1·5 between the breadths of successive whorls corresponds (as we see by our table on p. 534) to a constant angle of about 86°, or just such a spiral as we commonly meet with in the Ammonites

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XII, “The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera”; topic “Logarithmic spiral of foraminiferal shells”. Scope: fusulinid Foraminifera (Fusulina cylindrica, F. Böcki)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch12-05: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.76

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The exact ratio and angle give an unusually sharp test using standard morphometrics. Data are scattered among digitized fossil collections, so full species coverage may require compilation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure successive whorl breadths in digitized Fusulina sections, estimate ratios and spiral angles with uncertainty, and test constancy around 1.5 and 86 degrees. Confidence intervals excluding these values or showing ontogenetic drift would refute the numerical claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Section orientation and fossil deformation can bias breadth ratios.

PBDB occurrence records do not themselves contain whorl measurements.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The numerical target is unambiguous, so a handful of well-oriented sections could confirm or refute it. What is openly downloadable is an ontogenetic landmark set for related fusulinid genera, which can test whether expansion ratios near 1.5 are typical of that family but cannot substitute for Fusulina cylindrica and F. böcki. Discriminating power is high once those specimens are measured; assembling them is the limiting step.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure successive whorl breadths on oriented thin sections of Fusulina cylindrica and Fusulina böcki and convert a constant breadth ratio to a spiral angle. The claim is confirmed if the ratio clusters near 1.5 and the angle near 86° across whorls and specimens; a ratio that drifts with whorl number, or a mean far from 1.5, would refute the stated figures.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Published measurements of those species are scattered in monographs and would have to be redigitized from plates.

The open coordinate file does not contain the two named Fusulina species.
